questions.stem: How long without oxygen until permanent brain cell death begins?
questions.why: Permanent death of brain cells occurs after approximately 6 minutes without oxygen — the reason airway is always first.

options.why: Consciousness may be lost but cells survive longer than that.
Cells are stressed but not permanently dead that fast.
That is longer than brain cells survive anoxia.

questions.stem: What marks the boundary between the upper and lower airway?
questions.why: The larynx marks where the upper airway ends and the lower airway begins. The lower airway extends from the glottis to the pulmonary capillary membrane.

options.why: The cricoid is the lowest part of the larynx, not the boundary itself.
The epiglottis sits at the superior border of the glottis.
The carina is where the trachea bifurcates, well below.

questions.stem: Where is the cricothyroid membrane located?
questions.why: The cricothyroid membrane lies between the thyroid and cricoid cartilage — the site for emergency surgical and nonsurgical airway access, bordered laterally and inferiorly by the vascular thyroid gland.

options.t: Between the hyoid bone and thyroid cartilage
options.why: The thyrohyoid space is above the thyroid cartilage.

options.t: Between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages

options.why: The laryngeal prominence is the thyroid cartilage itself.

options.t: Between the cricoid ring and first tracheal ring
options.why: The cricoid IS the first tracheal ring.

questions.stem: What is the narrowest portion of the adult airway?
questions.why: The glottis — the space between the vocal cords — is the narrowest portion of the adult airway. ET intubation requires visualizing the epiglottis, glottis, and cords.

options.why: The nasal passage is not the narrowest airway point.
The cricoid ring is the narrowest point in small children.
The carina is a bifurcation, not a narrowing.

questions.stem: Which is true of the cricoid cartilage?
questions.why: The cricoid cartilage (cricoid ring) is the first ring of the trachea, forms the lowest portion of the larynx, and is more prominent in females.

options.why: The thyroid cartilage forms the laryngeal prominence.

options.t: It is the first ring of the trachea
It suspends the larynx from the hyoid
options.why: The thyroid ligament does that.

options.t: It is more prominent in males
options.why: The cricoid is more prominent in females.

questions.stem: What is external respiration?
questions.why: External (pulmonary) respiration exchanges O2 and CO2 between the alveoli and blood in the pulmonary capillaries. Internal (cellular) respiration is between systemic circulation and the cells.

options.t: Gas exchange between alveoli and pulmonary blood
Gas exchange between blood and the body's cells
options.why: That is internal (cellular) respiration.

options.t: The mechanical movement of air in and out

questions.stem: Which is an EARLY sign of hypoxia?
questions.why: Early hypoxia shows restlessness, irritability, apprehension, tachycardia, and anxiety. Late signs are mental status changes, weak pulse, and cyanosis. Give oxygen before signs appear.

options.why: That is a late sign.
Those are peri-arrest findings, beyond late hypoxia.
Those are late signs.

questions.stem: What is the most common airway obstruction in an unresponsive patient?
questions.why: The tongue is the most common obstruction in an unresponsive patient — with altered LOC it falls against the posterior pharyngeal wall.

options.why: Blood requires trauma or bleeding.
Food is the classic cause in responsive choking, not unresponsiveness.
Edema requires a triggering illness or injury.

questions.stem: What defines hypoventilation?
questions.why: Hypoventilation occurs when CO2 production exceeds elimination (hypercarbia results); hyperventilation is the reverse, lowering blood CO2 (hypocarbia).

options.why: That is hyperventilation.
Hypoventilation is defined by CO2, not oxygen.
Rate alone does not define it — a fast shallow rate can still hypoventilate.

questions.stem: Why might a patient with multiple rib fractures hypoventilate?
questions.why: Patients with rib fractures or flail chest purposely breathe shallowly to reduce pain — respiratory splinting — which decreases pulmonary ventilation.

options.why: The mechanism is behavioural, not alveolar damage.
Rib fractures do not swell the glottis.
The drive to breathe is intact — pain limits the effort.

questions.stem: What is intrapulmonary shunting?
questions.why: Nonfunctional alveoli inhibit diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide — blood flows past without gas exchange, called intrapulmonary shunting.

options.t: Blood bypassing the lungs through a septal defect
options.why: That is a cardiac shunt.

options.t: Redirection of blood away from the periphery
options.why: That is peripheral shunting in shock.

options.t: Air entering the pleural space under pressure
options.why: That is a tension pneumothorax.

questions.stem: Obstruction of blood flow that inhibits gas exchange is typically related to what?
questions.why: Obstruction of blood flow is typically trauma-related: simple/tension/open pneumothorax, hemothorax, hemopneumothorax, or pulmonary embolism.

options.why: That is a cellular metabolic factor.

options.t: Trauma, such as pneumothorax or hemothorax

options.why: Infection raises demand but does not obstruct flow.

options.t: High altitude lowering the oxygen partial pressure
options.why: That is an external environmental factor.

questions.stem: Both hemorrhagic and vasodilatory shock lead to what at the cellular level?
questions.why: Both forms of shock produce poor tissue perfusion that leads to anaerobic metabolism.

options.t: Improved oxygen extraction by peripheral tissues
options.why: Extraction cannot compensate for absent delivery.
Energy production falls without oxygen delivery.
Poor perfusion drives acidosis, not alkalosis.

questions.stem: What is the fastest way for the body to eliminate excess acid?
questions.why: The fastest way to eliminate excess acid is through the respiratory system — expelled as CO2 from the lungs. Slowing respirations raises CO2.

options.why: Lactic acid is itself an acid, not a disposal route.
Protein buffering is limited and slower.
Renal compensation takes hours to days.

questions.stem: An excessively high respiratory rate produces which disturbance?
questions.why: Alkalosis can develop if the rate or volume is too high, blowing off CO2. pH changes from bicarbonate are metabolic; from respiratory disorders, respiratory.

options.why: Metabolic disturbances stem from bicarbonate, not rate.
That reflects bicarbonate loss or acid gain, not breathing.
Acidosis follows inhibited respiratory function.

questions.stem: How does the renal system regulate pH?
questions.why: The renal system filters out more hydrogen and retains bicarbonate when needed, or does the reverse.

options.t: Producing extra carbon dioxide for exhalation
options.why: CO2 for exhalation comes from the bicarbonate buffer, not the kidney.

options.t: Storing excess acid within the medulla
options.why: Acid is excreted, not stored.
The kidney adjusts ions, not enzyme secretion into blood.

questions.stem: Secretions pooling in the mouth indicate what?
questions.why: Secretions pooling in the mouth indicate a markedly depressed or absent gag reflex, which significantly increases aspiration risk.

options.t: A depressed or absent gag reflex

options.why: Air may still move — the risk is aspiration.

options.t: An intact and hyperactive gag reflex
options.why: An intact gag would clear or react to the secretions.
Pooling secretions are a compromise sign, not reassurance.

questions.stem: What is the normal resting respiratory rate for an adult?
questions.why: Normal adult resting breathing: 12 to 20 breaths/min, adequate depth, regular pattern, clear and equal bilateral sounds.

options.why: Above 20 requires the same evaluation.
Below 12 requires evaluation for inadequate ventilation.
That range extends well into abnormal territory.

questions.stem: Which sign is described as a clear indicator of low blood oxygen?
questions.why: Cyanosis is a clear indicator of low blood oxygen. Preferential positioning — tripod or semi-Fowler — also signals distress.

options.why: Tachycardia is an early, nonspecific sign.
Restlessness is early and has many causes.
Sweating is nonspecific.

questions.stem: What is the correct order of airway management steps?
questions.why: Open the airway, clear the airway, assess breathing, then provide appropriate interventions — evaluated by observation, palpation, and auscultation.

options.why: Assessment of breathing follows a patent airway.
Intervention comes only after assessment.
You cannot clear an airway that is not yet opened.

questions.stem: What defines pulsus paradoxus?
questions.why: Pulsus paradoxus: systolic BP drops more than 10 mm Hg during inhalation — seen with increased intrathoracic pressure states like decompensating COPD, severe tamponade, tension pneumothorax, and severe asthma.

options.t: Systolic drop over 10 mm Hg on inhalation

options.why: Arm-to-arm comparison relates to dissection, not this.

options.t: Pulse rate rising sharply with each breath
options.why: Rate change with breathing is sinus arrhythmia.

options.t: Diastolic rise over 10 mm Hg on exhalation
options.why: The finding is a systolic drop during inhalation.

questions.stem: What is the physiologic purpose of sighing?
questions.why: A sigh — slow deep inhalation with prolonged exhalation — periodically hyperinflates the lungs, reexpanding atelectatic alveoli. The average person sighs about once per minute.

options.why: That describes hiccupping.
That is the eustachian tube's function.
Coughing clears the airways.

questions.stem: What is the normal inspiratory-to-expiratory (I/E) ratio?
questions.why: Expiration is normally at least twice as long as inspiration (1:2). Lower airway obstruction stretches it to 1:4 or 1:5; tachypnea shortens it toward 1:1.

options.why: Expiration is the longer phase, not inspiration.
1:4 to 1:5 indicates lower airway obstruction.
1:1 appears in tachypneic patients.

questions.stem: Which sound indicates mucus or fluid in the larger lower airways?
questions.why: Rhonchi are continuous, low-pitched sounds indicating mucus or fluid in the larger lower airways.

options.why: Crackles come from the smaller lower airways.
Wheezing is a constricted lower airway.
Stridor arises at or above the glottic opening.

questions.stem: Where does the problem lie when you hear stridor?
questions.why: Stridor — loud, high-pitched, typically inspiratory — results from foreign body, infection, swelling, disease, or trauma within or immediately above the glottic opening.

options.t: In the smaller peripheral airways of the lungs
options.why: Small-airway problems produce crackles or wheezes.

options.t: In the alveoli and terminal ducts
options.why: Alveolar fluid produces crackles.
Pleural inflammation produces a friction rub.

options.t: Within or just above the glottic opening

questions.stem: Which is true of late inspiratory crackles?
questions.why: Late inspiratory crackles occur when peripheral alveoli and airways pop open, more common in dependent lung regions. Early crackles occur as larger proximal bronchi open and are common in COPD.

options.t: They are common in patients with COPD
options.why: COPD is associated with the early type.

options.t: They clear completely after two or three coughs
options.why: Crackles that clear with coughing come from mobile secretions in the larger airways, not from alveoli popping open.

options.t: They occur as the proximal bronchi snap open
options.why: That describes early inspiratory crackles.

options.t: They occur as peripheral alveoli pop open

questions.stem: What causes a pleural friction rub?
questions.why: Inflammation thickens the pleura, and the visceral and parietal surfaces rub together — often causing stabbing pain with breathing or thoracic movement.

options.t: Spasmodic closure of the vocal cords
options.why: That is laryngospasm.

options.t: Air trapped in the subcutaneous tissue
options.why: That produces crepitus on palpation, not a rub on auscultation.

options.t: Fluid moving in the smaller lower airways
options.why: That produces crackles.

questions.stem: What does a pulse oximeter actually measure?
questions.why: A pulse oximeter measures the percentage of hemoglobin in arterial blood that is saturated with oxygen, assessing only pulsating vessels so it reads arterial rather than venous blood.

options.t: The oxygen dissolved in the plasma
options.why: Dissolved oxygen is a tiny fraction and is not measured.

options.t: The partial pressure of arterial oxygen
options.why: That is PaO2, from blood gas analysis.

options.t: The oxygen content of exhaled air
options.why: Exhaled gas is capnography territory.

questions.stem: Which SpO2 signals a need for aggressive oxygen therapy?
questions.why: A normally perfused person has SpO2 above 95% on room air; under 95% in a nonsmoker suggests hypoxemia, and under 90% signals a need for aggressive oxygen therapy.

options.why: Below 95% suggests hypoxemia but not yet the aggressive threshold.
93% is below the target but not the stated aggressive-therapy line.
98% is within normal.

questions.stem: Which can produce an erroneous pulse oximetry reading?
questions.why: Erroneous readings: bright ambient light, patient motion, poor perfusion, nail polish, venous pulsations (right heart failure), and abnormal hemoglobin. Cover the clip or move it to the earlobe or nose.

options.t: Bright ambient light on the sensor

options.why: Rate does not corrupt the optical measurement.
High FiO2 produces a genuinely high reading, not an error.
Glucose does not interfere with the light spectrum.

questions.stem: What is the normal EtCO2 range in a perfusing adult?
questions.why: Normal perfusing adults read 35–45 mm Hg; during cardiac arrest the target range is 10–20 mm Hg. EtCO2 runs about 2–5 mm Hg below arterial PaCO2.

options.why: 10 to 20 is the target during cardiac arrest.
Below 35 indicates hyperventilation.
Above 45 indicates hypoventilation.

questions.stem: When a colorimetric detector sees exhaled CO2, the paper turns which color?
questions.why: After 6 to 8 positive pressure breaths, the paper turns from purple to yellow during exhalation. Use for initial confirmation, then replace with a quantitative device — it degrades with temperature, humidity, and secretions.

options.why: The change runs purple to yellow, not the reverse.
Those are not the detector's colors.
Those are not the detector's colors.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a capnometer from a capnographer?
questions.why: A capnometer displays a numeric reading of exhaled CO2; a capnographer provides a graphic waveform representation.

options.why: Colorimetric is the qualitative paper detector, a third type.

options.t: Capnometer is numeric; capnographer is graphic
Capnometer is graphic; capnographer is numeric
options.why: The two are reversed here.

options.t: They are interchangeable names for one device
options.why: They display differently.

questions.stem: What is the recommended method for monitoring advanced airway placement?
questions.why: Quantitative waveform capnography is the recommended method of monitoring initial and ongoing placement of an advanced airway device.

options.why: Oximetry lags and does not confirm tube position.
Those are backups when capnography is unavailable.

options.t: A colorimetric CO2 detector left in place
options.why: Colorimetric is initial-confirmation only, then replaced.

questions.stem: Which phase of the capnographic waveform is the alveolar plateau?
questions.why: Phase I (A-B) is the respiratory baseline, Phase II (B-C) the expiratory upslope, Phase III (C-D) the alveolar plateau, Phase IV (D-E) the inspiratory downstroke.

options.why: Phase IV is the inspiratory downstroke.
Phase I is the respiratory baseline.
Phase II is the expiratory upslope.

questions.stem: What does hypoventilation look like on capnography?
questions.why: Hypoventilation: tall waveforms, EtCO2 over 45, prolonged plateau, longer intervals. Hyperventilation: small waveforms, under 35. Shark fin = bronchospasm; flat line = extubation or obstructed sampling line.

options.why: Waveform loss suggests inadvertent extubation.
Small waveforms with low values indicate hyperventilation.
Shark fin indicates bronchospasm with incomplete emptying.

questions.stem: An intubated patient's waveform suddenly reads zero and flattens. Beyond extubation, what else can cause this?
questions.why: Sampling tubing from the in-line adaptor can be obstructed with blood or debris, zeroing out the waveform — replace the in-line adaptor to restore it.

options.why: ROSC raises EtCO2 rather than erasing it.

options.t: Blood or debris blocking the sampling tube

options.why: Hyperventilation shrinks the waveform but does not zero it.
Bronchospasm produces a shark-fin shape, not a flat zero.

questions.stem: During cardiac arrest, capnography can indicate what?
questions.why: Capnography indicates chest compression effectiveness and detects return of spontaneous circulation. Prolonged arrest yields minimal exhaled CO2 from severe acidosis and poor CO2 return to the lungs.

options.why: Rhythm comes from the ECG.
pH requires blood gas analysis.
Duration cannot be read from the waveform.

questions.stem: An uninjured, unresponsive patient breathing adequately should be placed in which position?
questions.why: Nontrauma patients with decreased LOC who maintain their airway and breathe adequately go in the recovery position — left lateral recumbent.

options.why: Sniffing is for intubation, not maintenance.
Prone patients get log-rolled supine, not left prone.
Semi-Fowler suits responsive distressed patients.

questions.stem: Which is a contraindication to the head tilt–chin lift?
questions.why: Head tilt–chin lift is for unresponsive patients with no spinal mechanism who can't protect their airway; it's contraindicated in responsive patients and possible cervical spine injury — use the jaw thrust there.

options.why: An absent gag supports using the maneuver.
Unresponsiveness is an indication.
That is an indication.

questions.stem: Why can't the tongue-jaw lift be used while ventilating?
questions.why: The tongue-jaw lift is used to open the airway for suctioning or OPA insertion — it cannot be used to ventilate because it will not allow an adequate mask seal.

options.why: Gag response is a separate concern with adjuncts.
It involves no neck movement.
It lifts tissue away from the glottis.

options.t: It prevents an adequate mask seal

questions.stem: What is the maximum suctioning time for an adult?
questions.why: Maximum suction time: 15 seconds adult, 10 children, 5 infants. Suctioning removes oxygen — preoxygenate first, and stimulating the throat can trigger a vagal response.

options.why: 10 seconds is the limit for children.
5 seconds is the limit for infants.
30 seconds removes far too much oxygen.

questions.stem: Which catheter can be passed down an ET tube?
questions.why: Soft, nonrigid French/whistle-tip catheters can be placed in the oropharynx, nasopharynx, or down an ET tube, and suit the nose or the back of the mouth when a rigid catheter cannot be used.

options.t: Bare suction tubing without any catheter tip

questions.why: Measure from the corner of the mouth to the earlobe, and never insert a catheter past the base of the tongue.

questions.why: Insert to the predetermined depth without suction, then apply suction in a circular motion as you withdraw. Repeat as needed.

options.why: Insertion is done without suction.

questions.stem: In whom should an oropharyngeal airway be inserted?
questions.why: The OPA is for unresponsive patients with no gag reflex — it holds the tongue off the glottis and doubles as a bite block, but does not prevent aspiration. If the patient gags, remove it and prepare to suction.

options.why: An intact gag is a contraindication.

options.t: Unresponsive patients without a gag reflex

options.why: It will stimulate gagging and retching in responsive patients.

options.t: Any patient with an altered mental status
options.why: Altered patients with a gag get an NPA instead.

questions.stem: What happens if an oral airway is improperly sized or inserted?
questions.why: An improperly sized or inserted OPA can push the tongue into the pharynx and create an obstruction; rough insertion can injure the hard palate.

options.t: It can push the tongue back, obstructing
It seals the esophagus against aspiration
options.why: No adjunct at this level prevents aspiration.

options.t: It converts to nasal placement automatically
options.why: OPAs and NPAs are different devices.
Improper placement harms rather than helps.

questions.stem: Which finding contraindicates a nasopharyngeal airway?
questions.why: Do not use an NPA with nose trauma or suspected skull fracture. It is better tolerated than an OPA in patients with an intact gag but altered LOC, can be placed blindly, and can be suctioned through.

options.why: The NPA is well tolerated with an intact gag.

questions.stem: What is the typical foreign body airway obstruction victim?
questions.why: The typical victim is middle-aged or older, wears dentures, and has consumed alcohol — which depresses protective reflexes and impairs judgment about food size.

options.why: Sleeping children obstruct from the tongue, not foreign bodies.

options.t: A young healthy adult exercising vigorously
options.why: Exercise is not the classic setting — meals are.

questions.stem: What commonly causes laryngeal spasm?
questions.why: Laryngeal spasm — spasmodic vocal cord closure completely occluding the airway — is often caused by intubation trauma or occurs immediately on extubation. It may be relieved by aggressive ventilation or a forceful upward jaw pull.

options.t: Chronic exposure to dry inhaled gases
options.why: Dry gas irritates mucosa but is not the classic spasm trigger.

options.t: Slow progression of a viral infection
options.why: Infection more typically causes edema (epiglottitis).

options.t: Gradual growth of a laryngeal mass
options.why: Masses obstruct progressively rather than spasmodically.

questions.stem: Which are common causes of laryngeal edema?
questions.why: Laryngeal edema narrows or closes the glottic opening; common causes are epiglottitis, anaphylaxis, and inhalation injury.

options.why: Those are lung and pleural infections.

options.t: Rib fractures, flail chest, and pulmonary contusion
options.why: Those are chest wall injuries.

questions.stem: How should you manage a mild airway obstruction in a coughing patient?
questions.why: With mild obstruction the patient exchanges air and coughs — a forceful cough is the most effective dislodging mechanism. Intervening could force the object deeper. Monitor and be ready for signs of severe obstruction.

options.why: Thrusts are for severe obstruction.
They are moving air — support, don't ventilate.
Blind sweeps can push the object deeper.

options.t: Leave them alone and monitor closely

questions.stem: A choking patient becomes unresponsive. What do you do first?
questions.why: When the patient becomes unresponsive: supine, 30 chest compressions (15 with two rescuers for infant/child), open the airway, remove visible objects, attempt rescue breaths. If that fails, direct laryngoscopy and Magill forceps.

options.t: Perform abdominal thrusts with the patient supine
options.why: Thrusts end when responsiveness is lost.

options.t: Sweep the mouth blindly for the object
options.why: Remove only objects you can see.

questions.stem: In advanced pregnancy or morbid obesity, replace abdominal thrusts with what?
questions.why: If the patient is in the advanced stages of pregnancy or is morbidly obese, perform chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts.

options.why: Back blows are not the stated adult substitution.
Blind sweeps are never recommended.
Positioning does not expel an obstruction.

questions.stem: Which cylinder is typically carried from the ambulance to the patient?
questions.why: You'll most often use the D cylinder (350 L, carried to the patient) and the M cylinder (3,000 L, the ambulance's main supply). Delivery is measured in L/min.

questions.stem: What is the major disadvantage of the Bourdon-gauge flowmeter?
questions.why: The Bourdon-gauge flowmeter works in any position but does not compensate for backpressure — it usually reads falsely high when downstream flow is obstructed. The pressure-compensated flowmeter must stay upright.

options.t: It requires an external power source
options.why: Neither type needs external power.

questions.stem: What oxygen concentration does a nonrebreathing mask deliver?
questions.why: The NRB — preferred prehospital device — delivers 90–100% with a good seal at 15 L/min. Fill the reservoir first and keep flow at 12–15 L/min so the bag doesn't collapse. Contraindicated in apnea and poor respiratory effort.

That is the Venturi mask.

questions.stem: Which patient is the nasal cannula LEAST appropriate for?
questions.why: The cannula (1–6 L/min, 24–44%) is ineffective with apnea, poor respiratory effort, severe hypoxia, and mouth breathing. Humidify for prolonged use.

options.t: A stable patient on long-term oxygen

questions.stem: What is distinctive about the Venturi mask?
questions.why: The Venturi mask draws room air in with the oxygen and delivers 24%, 28%, 35%, or 40% depending on the adapter — most useful for hospital management of chronic respiratory disease and long-range transport.

options.why: It entrains room air but still needs oxygen flow.

questions.stem: Why does oxygen from a cylinder eventually need humidification?
questions.why: Cylinder oxygen has zero humidity and rapidly dries mucous membranes. A sterile-water humidifier bottle must stay upright (practical only on the fixed unit) and can be an infection source — use disposable bottles.

options.why: Cylinders store dry gas; nothing is added.

options.why: Gas exchange works regardless — mucosa drying is the issue.

questions.stem: How does positive pressure ventilation affect circulation?
questions.why: PPV needs more air for the same effect, pushes the chest walls out of shape, raises intrathoracic pressure, and decreases venous return — so less blood is pumped out. Regulate rate and volume carefully.

options.why: Reduced venous return lowers output, not raises it.

questions.stem: Why can overly forceful ventilation cause gastric distention?

questions.stem: What tidal volume produces visible chest rise in most adults?
questions.why: Deliver 500–600 mL (6–7 mL/kg) over 1 second — enough for visible chest rise. The adult bag holds 1,200–1,600 mL; pediatric 500–700; infant 150–240.

That is the infant bag's capacity.

questions.stem: How often do you squeeze the bag for an apneic adult with a pulse?
questions.why: Adults: every 5–6 seconds (10–12/min). Infants and children: every 3–5 seconds (12–20/min). Cardiac arrest, any age: every 6–8 seconds (8–10/min).

options.why: That is the infant and child interval.
That rate would badly over-ventilate.
That is the cardiac arrest interval.

questions.stem: What is the one-rescuer bag-mask hand position called?

questions.stem: Ventilating a patient, you notice the stomach rising and falling. What is the fix?
questions.why: Stomach movement means air is entering the esophagus — reposition the head (jaw only if spinal injury suspected). If air escapes, reposition the mask; if the chest still doesn't rise, check for obstruction.

options.why: Mask size affects the seal, not air routing.
Flow rate does not redirect where air goes.

options.why: Comfort preference doesn't change its physiologic limitations in severe cases.

options.t: Mild hypoxia in an alert, breathing patient
options.why: Mild hypoxia in an alert patient is exactly where a cannula works well.
Long-term home use is a classic appropriate cannula application.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a nonrebreather mask from a partial rebreathing mask?
questions.why: The nonrebreather's one-way valve prevents exhaled air from mixing back in; the partial rebreathing mask lacks that valve.

options.t: The partial rebreather actually delivers more oxygen than the other
options.why: The nonrebreather actually delivers a higher oxygen concentration, not less.

options.t: The nonrebreather is intended for apneic patients specifically
options.why: Nonrebreathers are for spontaneously breathing patients, not apneic ones.

options.t: The nonrebreather has a one-way valve that the partial one lacks
Only the partial rebreather is considered standard field equipment
options.why: Both devices are standard prehospital equipment.

questions.stem: What flow rate and delivered oxygen concentration does a nasal cannula typically provide?
questions.why: A nasal cannula runs 1–6 L/min and delivers roughly 24–44% oxygen — modest compared to mask devices.

options.why: That range describes a partial rebreathing mask.
Nearly 100% describes a BVM with an oxygen reservoir, not a cannula.
That describes a nonrebreather mask.

questions.stem: How should a tracheostomy patient needing supplemental oxygen be managed?
questions.why: With a tracheostomy, the stoma is the functional airway — oxygen or BVM ventilation is applied there, plugging the nose and mouth during bagging so air doesn't escape.

options.t: Cover the stoma itself with a mask or BVM, plugging nose and mouth
Ventilate through the mouth while an assistant occludes the stoma
options.why: That reverses it — the stoma is the airway, so it is the mouth and nose that get occluded.

options.t: Place a nasal cannula into the stoma and run it at 6 L/min
options.why: A cannula in the stoma cannot deliver ventilation or a reliable oxygen concentration — a mask or BVM goes over the stoma.

options.t: Deliver oxygen through the nose and mouth, ignoring the stoma entirely
options.why: Airflow needs to go through the stoma, since that's the patient's actual airway now.

questions.stem: When bagging a patient, how should the delivered tidal volume be judged?
questions.why: Visible chest rise is the practical, real-time indicator that a breath is adequate — not a fixed number or fully emptying the bag.

options.t: By a fixed volume regardless of patient size
options.why: A fixed volume ignores patient-to-patient differences in size and lung compliance.
Rate alone doesn't tell you whether each breath is adequate.

options.t: By squeezing the bag completely every time
options.why: Fully emptying the bag every time risks overinflation and gastric distention.

questions.stem: What causes gastric distention during bag-mask ventilation?
questions.why: Ventilating too hard or too fast pushes air past the esophagus into the stomach instead of the lungs, inflating it and risking vomiting.

options.t: Choosing a nasal cannula rather than a bag-mask device
options.why: A nasal cannula doesn't involve positive-pressure ventilation at all.

options.t: Proper technique guided carefully by watching for chest rise
options.why: Ventilating to visible chest rise, done correctly, is what avoids gastric distention in the first place.

options.t: Ventilating too hard or fast pushes air past the esophagus, not lungs
Suctioning performed on the patient before ventilation begins
options.why: Suctioning doesn't push air into the stomach.

questions.stem: Why is gastric distention dangerous during ventilation?
questions.why: A distended stomach pushes up on the diaphragm, restricting how much the lungs can expand, and increases the risk of vomiting and aspiration.

options.t: It has no clinical significance during a resuscitation
options.why: A distended stomach is a real problem worth correcting, not a neutral finding.

options.t: It pushes the diaphragm up, limiting lung expansion, and promotes vomiting
It automatically improves oxygenation by increasing intra-abdominal pressure
options.why: Increased abdominal pressure from a distended stomach does not improve oxygenation — it interferes with it.

options.t: It only matters in pediatric patients
options.why: Gastric distention is a risk in any age group receiving positive-pressure ventilation, not just pediatrics.

questions.stem: A previously well-ventilating intubated patient suddenly deteriorates. The DOPE mnemonic checks for which four causes?
questions.why: DOPE stands for Dislodgment, Obstruction, Pneumothorax, and Equipment failure — the four things to rule out when a tubed patient suddenly worsens.

options.t: Dyspnea, oxygenation status, positioning, and patient effort
options.why: That's a plausible-sounding list, but it's not the actual mnemonic used for sudden deterioration.

options.t: Distention, obstruction, perfusion status, and expiration rate
options.why: Perfusion and expiration aren't part of the DOPE checklist.

options.t: Dislodgment, obstruction, pneumothorax, and equipment failure
Dislodgment, oxygen supply, cuff pressure, and embolism
options.why: Pressure and embolism aren't the D-O-P-E letters as taught.

questions.stem: In DOPE, what does the 'D' stand for?
questions.why: D is for Dislodgment — the tube may have moved out of the trachea, into the esophagus, or too deep into a mainstem bronchus.

options.why: Desaturation is a finding you'd investigate using DOPE, not a letter in it.
Distention isn't one of the DOPE letters.
Dyspnea is a symptom, not part of this mnemonic.

questions.stem: In DOPE, what does the 'P' stand for?
questions.why: P is for Pneumothorax — positive-pressure ventilation can cause or worsen one, cutting off air movement on that side.

options.t: Pneumothorax risk, checked whenever ventilation gets harder
options.why: Positioning isn't the DOPE letter — dislodgment covers tube position separately.
Perfusion isn't part of this specific mnemonic.
Pressure alone isn't the DOPE letter, though equipment pressure issues fall under E.

questions.stem: In DOPE, what does the 'E' stand for?
questions.why: E is for Equipment failure — checking the oxygen source, tubing, and BVM itself when a ventilated patient decompensates.

options.t: Embolism, which isn't part of this particular mnemonic
options.why: Embolism isn't part of this mnemonic.

options.t: Expiration rate, which isn't one of the DOPE letters at all
options.why: Expiration isn't the DOPE letter.

options.t: Effort level, which isn't the E being referenced in DOPE
options.why: Effort isn't the E in DOPE.

options.t: Equipment failure — check the source, tubing, and the BVM itself

questions.stem: What is the primary physiologic effect of CPAP?
questions.why: CPAP delivers continuous positive pressure that pops open collapsed alveoli and pushes oxygen across the alveolar membrane, also forcing fluid back into circulation.

options.t: It seals the airway against aspiration the way a cuffed tube does
options.why: CPAP does not protect the airway at all — an inability to protect the airway is a contraindication to using it.

options.t: It actually decreases the pressure inside the chest cavity
options.why: CPAP increases intrathoracic pressure, not decreases it.

options.t: It opens collapsed alveoli and pushes O2 across the membrane wall
It raises preload by driving blood back toward the right heart
options.why: Positive intrathoracic pressure reduces venous return and preload rather than raising it.

questions.stem: Which finding supports starting CPAP?
questions.why: CPAP is used for a patient in respiratory distress, breathing 26+ times per minute, with a pulse ox below 90% — and who is alert enough to follow commands.

options.t: A rate of 26 or more breaths a minute with a pulse ox under 90%
A shock patient in cardiogenic shock with a systolic of 70
options.why: Significant hypotension is a contraindication to CPAP, not an indication.

options.t: A completely normal rate of 12 with a pulse ox of 98 percent
options.why: Normal rate and saturation don't indicate a need for CPAP.

options.t: An unresponsive patient breathing with agonal gasps only
options.why: CPAP requires an alert patient who can follow commands — agonal, unresponsive patients need a different intervention.

questions.stem: Why must a CPAP patient be alert and able to follow commands?
questions.why: CPAP depends on the patient actively breathing against the mask pressure and being able to protect their own airway — an unresponsive patient can't do either safely.

options.t: CPAP is uncomfortable and needs a fresh verbal consent every breath
options.why: Discomfort isn't the reason — it's a physiologic necessity for the mask to work as intended.

options.t: CPAP needs patient cooperation and effort against the mask pressure
Alertness level changes which pressure setting gets dialed in
options.why: Alertness doesn't change the pressure setting itself.

options.t: It's simply a legal requirement, unrelated to the physiology
options.why: This is a physiologic and safety requirement, not simply a legal formality.

questions.stem: Why can CPAP cause hypotension?
questions.why: CPAP's positive pressure can reduce blood flow to the brain; the brain then demands more oxygen and shunts blood to itself, which can drop peripheral blood pressure.

options.t: Increased pressure reduces cerebral blood flow, causing central shunting
No connection to blood pressure has ever been documented
options.why: CPAP has a well-documented hypotension risk through this central pressure mechanism.

options.t: CPAP reduces cardiac muscle contractility on its own
options.why: CPAP's hypotension mechanism runs through pressure and shunting, not a direct hit to contractility.

options.t: CPAP directly dilates all the peripheral blood vessels
options.why: CPAP's pressure effect is central, not a direct vasodilating action on the periphery.

questions.stem: What is a known complication of CPAP therapy?
questions.why: The positive pressure CPAP generates can cause a pneumothorax, one of its recognized risks.

options.why: Venous return is often reduced by increased intrathoracic pressure, not improved.
Gastric emptying isn't a described CPAP effect.
CPAP tends toward increasing rate concerns, not slowing breathing as a complication.

questions.stem: What is PEEP?
questions.why: PEEP — positive end-expiratory pressure — is the resistance maintained at the end of exhalation, keeping alveoli from collapsing.

options.t: Peak inspiratory pressure measured at the very start of a breath
options.why: Peak inspiratory pressure is a related but distinct value (PIP), measured on inhalation, not exhalation.

options.t: Positive pressure the patient exhales against at the end of a breath
The absolute maximum pressure any ventilator device can generate
options.why: PEEP is not defined as an equipment ceiling — it's a therapeutic exhalation pressure.

options.t: A saturation measurement taken during the exhalation phase
options.why: PEEP is a pressure value, not an oxygen saturation measurement.

questions.stem: What is the normal PEEP range in healthy lungs?
questions.why: Normal healthy lungs maintain roughly 3–5 cm H2O of PEEP, whether occurring naturally or set on a device.

options.why: 10–15 cm H2O is therapeutic PEEP set on a device, not what a healthy lung holds on its own.
20–25 cm H2O is a ventilator setting reserved for severe ARDS — far above any physiologic baseline.
0 would mean no end-expiratory pressure at all, not the normal physiologic baseline.

questions.stem: An intubated patient who was ventilating well suddenly drops to a flat, near-zero capnography trace. Chest rise is absent. What is the FIRST thing to rule out?
questions.why: A sudden flat-zero capnogram with no chest rise points to the tube no longer being in the trachea. DOPE is worked in order, and D — dislodgment — is ruled out first.

options.t: Tube dislodgment out of the trachea

options.why: Pneumothorax typically leaves some CO2 return and unilateral findings.
An obstruction usually dampens the waveform rather than flattening it to zero.

options.t: Equipment failure at the oxygen source
options.why: Equipment failure is on the DOPE list but is checked after tube position.

questions.stem: A CPAP patient becomes progressively hypotensive ten minutes into treatment. What best explains this?
questions.why: Positive pressure raises intrathoracic pressure, which reduces venous return and therefore stroke volume and cardiac output — the classic mechanism behind CPAP-associated hypotension.

options.t: Rising chest pressure is cutting venous return
CPAP is directly dilating peripheral vessels
options.why: CPAP has no direct peripheral vasodilating action of its own.

options.t: Oxygen toxicity is developing from the therapy
options.why: Oxygen toxicity does not develop over a ten-minute prehospital course.

options.t: The mask seal has failed and pressure is lost
options.why: A lost seal would reduce therapeutic effect, not drive blood pressure down.

questions.stem: A patient's capnogram shows unusually tall waveforms with an EtCO2 of 58 mmHg. What does this indicate, and what is the correction?
questions.why: Tall waveforms with elevated EtCO2 mean CO2 is accumulating faster than it is cleared. The fix is more effective ventilation to blow off the excess.

options.t: Esophageal placement — remove and reattempt the tube
options.why: Esophageal placement gives little or no CO2 return, not an elevated reading.

options.t: Hypoventilation — increase rate and depth of ventilation
Hyperventilation — slow the assisted ventilation rate
options.why: Hyperventilation produces small waveforms with a low EtCO2, the opposite finding.

options.t: Normal ventilation — no change to management needed
options.why: An EtCO2 of 58 is well above the 35–45 normal range, so this is not normal.

questions.stem: You are suctioning an adult whose SpO2 falls from 92% to 78% partway through. What is the correct action?
questions.why: Suctioning removes oxygen along with secretions. The 15-second limit is a ceiling, not a target — significant desaturation means stop and reoxygenate immediately.

options.t: Switch to a smaller-bore suction catheter
options.why: Catheter size will not reverse a desaturation already in progress.

options.t: Stop suctioning and reoxygenate the patient
Increase the suction pressure to finish faster
options.why: Raising pressure worsens the oxygen removal that is causing the drop.

options.t: Continue to the full 15-second time limit
options.why: Finishing the full window ignores that the patient is already desaturating badly.

questions.stem: You are bagging a tracheostomy patient through the stoma but get poor chest rise. What should you check first?
questions.why: With a stoma, air delivered below the larynx can escape upward and out the nose and mouth. Occluding them directs the volume into the lungs and restores chest rise.

options.t: Whether an OPA has been correctly sized
options.why: An oral airway is irrelevant when ventilating through a surgical stoma.

options.t: Whether the nose and mouth are plugged
Whether the head is in a sniffing position
options.why: Head positioning matters for an upper airway, which the stoma bypasses.

options.t: Whether the patient has an intact gag reflex
options.why: Gag reflex governs OPA use, not air escaping around a stoma.
